title: Maximum of three
instructorPromptText: Write a program that asks the user for three numbers, then prints the largest one. Do not use the built-in max() — decide with conditionals.

specGateDimensions.description: Are the three inputs expected to be integers, floats, or either? How should the program convert the raw input() strings?
specGateDimensions.rationale: input() returns strings; the student must commit to a conversion (int vs float) before writing code, or comparisons will silently misbehave (string comparison) or crash.

specGateDimensions.description: If two or all three numbers are equal to the maximum, what does the program print — the value once, a message about the tie, or something else?
specGateDimensions.rationale: The prompt says 'the largest one' as if it is unique. Ties are the canonical missed case for max-of-N problems and the conditional structure the student picks depends on this commitment.

specGateDimensions.description: Will the spec describe comparing all three at once (nested/compound conditionals) or tracking a running maximum across pairwise comparisons?
specGateDimensions.rationale: The prompt forbids max() and mandates conditionals, so the student must commit to a decision strategy in the spec rather than discovering it while typing.

specGateDimensions.description: What should happen if the user types something that isn't a number?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Forces the student to either commit to 'assume valid input' explicitly or plan for conversion errors, rather than letting a crash count as undefined behavior.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Student forgets int()/float() conversion and compares strings, so '9' > '10' returns True and the wrong number prints for multi-digit inputs
Spec commits to handling ties with a special message, but code just prints one value because the tie branch was never written

Chained conditional misses a case — e.g. `if a > b and a > c: print(a); elif b > c: print(b); else: print(c)` works, but a variant like `if a > b: if a > c: print(a)` drops the case where b is largest
Uses `>` strictly where `>=` was needed (or vice versa) and gets no output when two numbers tie for the maximum
Plan describes three-way nested conditionals; code uses a running-maximum pattern (largest = a; if b > largest: largest = b; ...) — coherent restructure that still satisfies the no-max() constraint
Student calls input() once with a single prompt expecting three space-separated numbers, when spec said three separate prompts (or vice versa)
